text:
Recent work supports separating persistent preferences from current intent, but does not establish an optimal recent window for this benchmark. [FSASA (2024)](https://www.comsis.org/archive.php?show=ppr906-2305) combines global SASRec representations with local session-aware representations through GRU weighting. [MiaSRec (SIGIR 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00986) challenges last-item dominance: it builds item-centered intent representations and dynamically selects relevant ones. [DICSI (2025)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-025-00650-w) uses multi-level temporal convolutions and cross-session intent fusion, offering mechanisms for tracking intent at several temporal scales.

[DSASR (2026)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-02282-0) is especially close to the proposed direction: separate causal short-/long-term transformers, with cosine disagreement informing an adaptive fusion gate. Its demographic inputs are unavailable here; its Amazon Beauty results do not establish transfer to the four pinned categories. A lightweight hypothesis inspired by these approaches: retain SASRec, maintain a persistent prefix mean and an adaptive short-term state, and learn a reset gate from current-item/state disagreement plus observed timestamp gaps. Compute every state using only the available prefix; “causal” here means no future leakage, not identified causal effects.

Evaluate this hypothesis against uniform prefix pooling, fixed-window pooling, and fixed-decay averaging under identical training and pinned macro validation HR@10. Ablate reset and fusion gates separately to distinguish useful intent adaptation from extra capacity. Missing history-edit diagnostics leave recency dependence unverified; the papers motivate these comparisons, rather than proving adaptive segmentation will improve sparse Amazon recommendation.
